nameStory: The Arched Hooktip gets its name from the distinctive curved, hook-like tips of its forewings that arch gracefully when the moth is at rest. This elegant curve gives the moth a crescent moon appearance, making it instantly recognizable among New England's night fliers. The 'arched' part refers to how these hooked wings create a beautiful bow shape when folded.
description: The Arched Hooktip is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan ranging from about 1 to 1.5 inches across. Its most striking feature is the curved, hook-shaped tips of its forewings that give it an unmistakable crescent silhouette when resting. The moth has muted brown and gray coloring that helps it blend perfectly against tree bark during the day. You'll spot adults flying from mid-May through late July, with just one generation per year in our New England climate.

idTips.label: Hooked wing tips
idTips.description: The forewings end in distinctive curved hooks that arch gracefully backward, creating a crescent moon shape when the moth is at rest

idTips.label: Size and wingspan
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wings spanning roughly 1 to 1.5 inches across, about the size of a quarter when fully spread

idTips.label: Coloration pattern
idTips.description: Muted brown and gray tones with subtle darker and lighter bands across the wings that feel soft and powdery to the touch

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a tent-like position with the hooked tips creating an unmistakable arched silhouette

idTips.label: Flight timing
idTips.description: Active from mid-May through late July, typically coming to lights on warm, humid evenings

habitat: Look for Arched Hooktips in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges where paper birch and alder trees grow, as these are the host plants for their caterpillars. They're especially common in moist areas like stream valleys, pond edges, and boggy woodlands where alders thrive. You'll find them throughout New England's forested regions, from lowland areas up into the mountains wherever their host trees are present.

seasonality.spring: Late spring is when the first adults begin emerging in mid-May, often attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting on warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through June and July when adults are most commonly seen flying and mating. Look for the distinctive caterpillars building their communal silk shelters on birch and alder leaves.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight period ends by late July, and the species overwinters as pupae. You might find old silk shelters on deciduous trees as leaves fall.
seasonality.winter: Moths are in pupal stage underground or in protected spots, completely hidden from view until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: The caterpillars of Arched Hooktips are nature's little drummers - they actually make music by shaking their bodies, drumming with their heads, and scraping their mouthparts against leaves to communicate with other caterpillars and attract them to their communal silk shelters!
confusionNotes: The hooked wing tips make this moth nearly impossible to confuse with other species - no other common New England moth has such distinctly curved forewings. If you see the characteristic hooks, you've found an Arched Hooktip!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'hooktip,' this moth is actually more closely related to silk moths than to the typical moths most people think of, which is why it has such a distinctive wing shape and resting posture.
compareHints: The Arched Hooktip is the only member of its genus found in New England, making identification straightforward. Compared to other moths in the Drepanidae family, it's distinguished by having the most pronounced wing hooks and the most distinctive crescent-shaped resting posture. While other hooktip moths exist elsewhere, none share this species' combination of size, coloring, and dramatically curved wing tips.
